question: Vertical Integration by Necessity
content: Max Hodak describes his approach to building Science's biohybrid brain interface: when critical components can't be bought off the shelf, you have to build them yourself. This means owning a MEMS foundry on the East Coast because no vendor could do the type of packaging and assembly required.
description: Your hardware startup needs a custom sensor that no existing vendor can manufacture to your specifications. The board suggests outsourcing the design and accepting compromises. Based on Max Hodak's approach at Science, what alternative strategy should you consider?
options: Accept vendor compromises to stay focused on your core product
Vertically integrate — own the manufacturing capability yourself if no
Redesign your product to work with off-the-shelf components exclusively
Partner with a larger company that already has the manufacturing capability
answer: Vertically integrate — own the manufacturing capability yourself if no
explanation: Max says: 'We own a captive MEMS foundry on the East Coast. There was no other way to do the type of packaging and assembly we wanted to do.' When components aren't available, vertical integration is the only path to real innovation.

question: AI's Hidden Impact: Regulatory
content: Max Hodak reveals that one of the biggest impacts AI has had inside Science is not in engineering but in regulatory interactions. AI can navigate the thousands of ISO standards that apply to a product, something that used to require a whole regulatory and quality team for several months.
description: Your medical device company is preparing for FDA audit. The regulatory team estimates six months to trace which ISO standards apply to your new product. Based on Max Hodak's experience at Science, where should you look for a faster solution?
options: Hire a larger regulatory and compliance team to parallelize the standards research across multiple domain experts
Deploy AI to trace applicable standards — it can navigate the complex regulatory landscape efficiently reveals biggest
Ignore the ISO standards that do not seem directly relevant to your product to save time and regulatory expense
Outsource the entire compliance verification work to a European notified body that specializes in medical devices
answer: Deploy AI to trace applicable standards — it can navigate the complex regulatory landscape efficiently reveals biggest
explanation: Max says: 'If we can generate documentation, or if we can ask — we want to evolve this product, there are thousands of ISO standards that might apply, which ones do we have to comply with — that used to require a whole regulatory and quality team for several months. Now the AI just kind of knows.'

question: Software Still Needs Hands
content: Max Hodak argues that even as AI becomes smarter than humans, there are real boundaries created by the physical world. AI can design a perfect chip or surgical device, but it still needs human hands — or robotic hands — to fabricate it in the physical world.
description: Your AI designs an optimal surgical tool with perfect simulations, but the design exists only as digital files. According to Max Hodak, what is the critical boundary that limits AI's impact in the physical world?
options: AI cannot generate valid STEP files or PCB layouts yet because those formats require precise physical specifications
The software still needs hands — if AI can't make things, that's
Robotic fabrication still lags behind AI design — physical reality imposes real constraints
AI-generated physical product designs are always inferior to those created by experienced human engineers and designers
answer: The software still needs hands — if AI can't make things, that's
explanation: Max says: 'Ultimately the software still needs hands. It's going to be smarter than us, but if it can't make things, those are real boundaries.' Even superhuman AI is constrained by its inability to manipulate the physical world.

question: Humans Become Verifiers
content: Naval synthesizes a pattern across engineering, law, and operations: humans are moving from being the primary doers of work to being verifiers of AI-generated output. The same way AI models are trained with human verification data, organizations now need human verifiers for AI output.
description: Your engineering team generates code through AI agents and then reviews the output before shipping. A board member asks why you still need engineers if AI does the coding. According to Naval's framework, what is the engineers' new primary function?
options: Engineers are now primarily prompt engineers who refine AI inputs
Engineers are becoming verifiers — standing behind the output
Engineers are transitioning to a project management role
Engineers are needed only for legacy system maintenance
answer: Engineers are becoming verifiers — standing behind the output
explanation: Naval says: 'Humans are becoming verifiers. That's how we train these models — with good verification data — and now we need human verifiers.' The human's role shifts from writing code to verifying AI output and taking responsibility for it.

question: The Great Promotion
content: Naval draws a parallel between software engineering and law: AI doesn't eliminate jobs — it eliminates the junior version of the job, effectively promoting everyone. Junior engineers become senior engineers; paralegals become lawyers — because the grunt work is now handled by AI.
description: Your law firm is debating whether to lay off junior associates after adopting an AI that can draft basic legal documents. A partner argues the AI makes junior lawyers obsolete. Based on Naval's 'great promotion' reframe, what is the alternative perspective?
options: Junior lawyers should be fired because their work can be done cheaper
Paralegals just got promoted to senior lawyers and can now spend
AI will replace all lawyers within five years regardless of seniority
Junior lawyers should shift to a career in software engineering instead
answer: Paralegals just got promoted to senior lawyers and can now spend
explanation: Naval says: 'Paralegals just got fired, or paralegals just got promoted to senior lawyers, and now they can spend their time thinking about the law.' The grunt work is gone; the human moves up the value chain to higher-order thinking and judgment.

question: The Trusted Authority
content: Guillermo Rauch draws a parallel between law and software: what you value in a lawyer is their willingness to put their reputation on the line. The same is becoming true for engineers — their value is not in writing code but in signing off on the consequences of deploying code.
description: A client asks your engineering firm to verify that a critical infrastructure deployment is safe. They don't ask to see every line of code — they ask for your personal sign-off. What does Guillermo Rauch identify as the parallel between this scenario and legal practice?
options: Clients always want to read every line of code, just like every line of a contract
What you're valuing is a trusted authority who puts their reputation on the line
Engineers should never sign off on code they didn't personally write
The law requires engineers to provide a full code audit in every contract
answer: What you're valuing is a trusted authority who puts their reputation on the line
explanation: Guillermo draws the parallel: 'What you're valuing in the relationship with a lawyer is that they're a trusted authority. They went to law school. They're putting their reputation on the line.' The same applies to engineers verifying AI output.

question: The Mountain of Slop
content: Guillermo Rauch identifies a major problem in the age of AI-generated code: the mountain of PR slop. Engineers receive pull requests where AI has generated most of the code, and the traditional expectation of reading every line becomes impractical.
description: Your team receives a 2000-line pull request that was 90% generated by AI. A senior engineer insists on reading every single line before approving. According to Guillermo Rauch, what is a more practical approach to code review in the AI era?
options: Every line of code must be read and understood before approval — no shortcuts
Engineers should write test harnesses, simulations, and proofs that identifies major problem
AI-generated code doesn't need review because the model is accountable
Only review the files that the AI model flagged as high-risk
answer: Engineers should write test harnesses, simulations, and proofs that identifies major problem
explanation: Guillermo says: 'I wrote the test harness, the simulations, the proofs, the type-checkers — even without reading this, I have confidence I can sign off that it'll be safe in production.' The confidence comes from the testing infrastructure, not line-by-line reading.

question: 1000 Days From Now
content: Guillermo Rauch warns that while AI makes creating software incredibly easy, the hard part is maintaining it for the long term. Creating software is zero to one, but what does the software look like 1000 days later? Is it secure, tested, production-grade, performant?
description: Your team churns out features rapidly using AI coding tools. After six months, the codebase is a tangled mess with no tests and no documentation. According to Guillermo Rauch, what aspect of software engineering is being dangerously neglected?
options: The team should switch to a different AI coding tool for better output
Creating software is easy — the hard part is maintaining it for 1000
The codebase quality doesn't matter as long as features ship on time
AI will automatically refactor and maintain the codebase without human input
answer: Creating software is easy — the hard part is maintaining it for 1000
explanation: Guillermo asks: 'Think about a thousand days from now. What does your software look like? Is it secure? Is it tested? Is it production-grade? Is it performant?' The ease of creation masks the long-term burden of maintenance.

question: Someone Gets Paged
content: Guillermo Rauch emphasizes that while AI can create software, someone still has to be responsible when things go wrong in production. The infrastructure production engineer who gets paged at 3 AM is the ultimate human accountability layer.
description: Your startup deploys AI-generated code directly to production without a dedicated operations team. A board member asks who is responsible when a deployment causes an outage. What does Guillermo Rauch argue is the human cost of AI-generated software?
options: The AI model provider is contractually liable for all production outages caused by their generated code output
Someone is going to get paged if your systems go down — there is no
Production outages are acceptable and expected in the age of rapid AI-driven software iteration and deployment
AI agents will self-heal production systems automatically without any need for human intervention or oversight
answer: Someone is going to get paged if your systems go down — there is no
explanation: Guillermo says: 'Someone is going to get paged if your systems go down.' The human accountability layer — the person who gets woken up at 3 AM — remains essential even as AI generates more of the code.

question: The Knowledge Gap in N-of-1 Medicine
content: Guillermo Rauch connects the democratization of AI to personalized medicine. Sid's story of N-of-1 cancer treatment required tremendous patient agency at a moment of weakness. AI could democratize access to this kind of personalized medical knowledge.
description: A family member is diagnosed with a rare condition and the standard treatment options are limited. You have resources to explore personalized approaches but lack medical expertise. How does Guillermo Rauch see AI changing this situation?
options: AI should not be trusted with medical decisions because of hallucination risks
AI could democratize the knowledge and research that goes into personalized
Personalized medicine will always require a team of specialist doctors
The FDA strictly prohibits AI involvement in any medical treatment decisions
answer: AI could democratize the knowledge and research that goes into personalized
explanation: Guillermo says about Sid's story: 'It requires a ton of agency from the patient in a moment where they're at their weakest. This is where AI should really shine, and democratize what you can actually do.' AI could make N-of-1 medicine accessible beyond the wealthy.
